short: Israel has no AI act: its December 2023 AI policy prefers sector regulators and soft regulation to a horizontal law. The binding layer is the Privacy Protection Law, whose Amendment 13, in force since 14 August 2025, gave the regulator monetary sanctions.
title: Israel AI Laws
subtitle: No AI act by policy: sector regulators and the amended Privacy Protection Law
body_html:
Status at a glance

No AI act, by policy. Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and Ethics, issued by the Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology and the Ministry of Justice on 17 December 2023, deliberately prefers sector-specific, risk-based and "soft" regulation, aligned with the OECD principles, to a horizontal AI law. The binding layer is the Privacy Protection Law, 5741-1981, transformed by Amendment No. 13: approved by the Knesset on 5 August 2024 and in force since 14 August 2025, it gives the Privacy Protection Authority administrative monetary sanctions. Verified on 25 October 2026 against the ministry's policy documents and the Privacy Protection Authority.

Key instruments

InstrumentNumberPassed or issuedIn force
Israel's Policy on Artificial Intelligence Regulation and EthicsMinistry of Innovation, Science and Technology and Ministry of Justice17 December 2023Policy, not law
Privacy Protection Law (Amendment No. 13)Privacy Protection Law 5741-1981, Amendment 13, 5784-2024Approved by the Knesset 5 August 202414 August 2025

Who regulates and enforces

  • Privacy Protection Authority: monetary sanctions and administrative inquiry under the amended law.
  • Ministry of Innovation, Science and Technology: leads AI policy, with an AI Policy Coordination Center.
  • Sector regulators apply their own rules to AI, as the 2023 policy directs.

Scope and reach

The Privacy Protection Law applies to database controllers and processors. No explicit territorial clause was found in the text reviewed.

Core obligations

  • The AI policy (not binding): sector-specific, risk-based regulation and ethical principles.
  • The Privacy Protection Law: notice (Art. 11), purpose limitation (Art. 8), a data security officer (Art. 17B) and a data protection officer (Art. 17B1) where required.

Penalties

BreachMaximumProvisionEnforcer
Processing for an unlawful purpose, without authorisation, or against a cease orderNIS 4 per person in the database (NIS 8 for data of special sensitivity), at least NIS 200,000PPL Art. 23KF(e)Head of the Privacy Protection Authority
No data protection or data security officer, and similar breachesNIS 2 per person (NIS 4 for sensitive data), at least NIS 20,000 (NIS 40,000)PPL Art. 23KF(d)Privacy Protection Authority
Registration and notification failuresNIS 150,000, doubled where the database holds 1,000,000 people or morePPL Art. 23KF(a)Privacy Protection Authority
Failing to provide documentsNIS 300,000PPL Art. 23KF(g)Privacy Protection Authority
Any sanctionReduced to 5% of the violator's turnover on requestPPL Schedule 5, s. 7Privacy Protection Authority

The amounts are as the Privacy Protection Authority's own unofficial English translation states them; the official Hebrew text in the Reshumot gazette governs.

What is coming next

No AI bill has been announced. The Knesset's legislation index is watched weekly.

How the policy works in practice

The 2023 policy sets six ethical principles and a Responsible Innovation framework, and leaves the law to the sector regulators: the Bank of Israel and the Israel Securities Authority for finance, the Ministry of Health for medical devices, and the Ministry of Justice's Office of Legal Counsel and Legislative Affairs for how tort, contract and administrative law reach AI. It proposed a national forum of regulators and experts to keep that sectoral work coherent, and it followed a 2022 White Paper on AI and a 2022 Ministry of Justice interpretive opinion on copyright and machine learning. Because there is no AI act, there are no AI-specific fines; every penalty comes from an existing statute.

The statute that matters is the Privacy Protection Law as amended. On 30 April 2025 the Privacy Protection Authority published for consultation a draft guidance on the application of the Privacy Protection Law to AI systems, which sets out the authority's reading of transparency, consent, data minimisation and automated decision duties as they apply to training and deploying AI, and which it stated would be the basis for its enforcement under Amendment No. 13. Law firms Pearl Cohen, Barnea Jaffa Lande and EBN report that the authority has since begun market-wide enforcement, that its first priorities are the new duty to appoint a data protection officer, on which it issued separate draft guidance, and the obligation on boards to oversee data processing, and that enforcement is expected to intensify through 2026. A draft National Cybersecurity Law published in January 2026 would add a second enforcement authority with reach over AI systems that hold Israeli data; it is a bill, not law.

What this means for a deployer: an AI system that touches personal data of people in Israel is now subject to administrative fines and, for unauthorised processing, criminal exposure under Amendment No. 13, with the authority's AI guidance as the yardstick even while it remains a draft. The 2023 policy's preference for soft regulation describes the AI-specific layer only; the privacy layer is hard law and actively enforced.

Last verified

4 November 2026, against the sources above. The AI guidance draft, the enforcement reports and the cybersecurity bill are as law firms report them, not read on gov.il, and are reported rather than verified. Not confirmed on an official source: whether the 2023 AI policy was adopted by a government decision, and whether the AI guidance has been finalised.
